screens.title: Functional Debugging and Performance Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: In embedded systems we often cannot look inside the running program the way we do on a desktop. This chapter equips you with practical techniques to observe what your code actually does, measure how long functions take, and stop errors before they cascade. You will learn functional debugging: building small test tables, running them on the hardware, and dumping results to the serial port or debugger to verify correctness. You will also learn how to use the processor SysTick timer to measure execution time in clock cycles, how to interpret those counts, and when wraparound matters. Finally, you will add simple assertion checks that report failures immediately during development. These techniques are complementary: test tables give you functional confidence, SysTick gives you quantitative performance data, and assertions let you catch invalid states early. Together they make embedded debugging systematic instead of accidental. As you proceed, keep a small test harness and a short timing routine handy. That combination will save hours verifying behavior on hardware. Consider which of these you will try first on your next lab board.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you'll learn four practical skills that make embedded debugging reliable. First, functional debugging: you'll build small test tables that capture inputs, expected outputs, and actual outputs, then run them on hardware and dump the results to the serial port. This gives repeatable evidence that a function behaves correctly for representative inputs. Second, you will measure execution time using the SysTick hardware timer. You will initialize the timer, sample its current value before and after a call, and compute the difference in clock cycles. Third, you'll analyze function performance by counting clock cycles across inputs to see how cost scales. This is how you move from guesswork to data-driven optimization. Fourth, you'll implement assertion macros that report the failing line and halt execution during development so errors are detected immediately. Each objective ties to hands-on checks: a test harness, a short timing routine, cycle-count comparisons, and an assertion-enabled build. These are concrete practices you can add to everyday embedded workflows to save debugging time and avoid subtle runtime errors.

screens.title: What is Functional Debugging?
screens.narratorSegment: Functional debugging is a pragmatic strategy to make program behavior visible on devices without rich UI or file systems. At its core you construct a small table of test cases: each entry records the input, the expected output, a slot for actual output, and a pass flag. You run the tests on the target hardware, populate actual outputs, and then transmit the table over the serial port or inspect it in the debugger. This approach turns an invisible internal computation into concrete, repeatable evidence. For example, a temperature conversion function can be validated by providing five known analog readings and their correct temperatures; after running the harness you will immediately see which entries match and which do not. A common misconception is that functional debugging replaces unit testing frameworks; instead it is a form of unit testing adapted for hardware constraints. The value is that you can reproduce edge cases on the real device and see real outputs rather than simulated results. Key practice: keep test cases small, deterministic, and representative so failures point directly to the function under test. How will you structure your first test table?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Functional debugging makes black-box behavior observable by recording inputs and outputs, then dumping them for inspection.

content.html:
Core Concept
Functional debugging
Record inputs and expected outputs, execute on hardware, and inspect results to locate faults.
  • Make a compact, structured test table that your firmware can iterate.
  • Populate actual outputs by calling the function under test for each entry.
  • Dump results to UART or view the array in a debugger to determine pass/fail.
  • Keep tests deterministic to make failures reproducible on hardware.
Common misconception
People think printing values is always too slow; while true for tight loops, strategic dumps after test runs give reliable evidence without changing program logic.
Key Takeaway

Functional debugging converts hidden state into a small, inspectable dataset so you can confirm function correctness on hardware.

Example test table (visual)
TestCase tests[5] = { {0,0,0,0}, {512,25,0,0}, {1023,50,0,0}, {256,12,0,0}, {768,37,0,0} };
After running runTests(), each actualOutput and passed field is populated. Dump the array to UART to see which cases failed.
Scenario
If test two fails, the UART will show expected 25 but actual 24. That points you to conversion rounding or calibration tables in the conversion function.

screens.title: Implementing a Test Table
screens.narratorSegment: Let's review a compact implementation pattern for a test table and the run loop that populates actual outputs. The pattern uses a small struct with four fields: input, expected output, actual output, and a pass flag. You initialize an array of these structs with known inputs and expected results, leaving actual output and the pass flag unset. The run loop calls the function under test for each input, stores the returned value in actual output, then compares it to expected to set the pass flag. This approach is explicit and easy to inspect on hardware. One practical tip is to keep the table small—five to ten representative cases—so the UART dump remains readable. A common error is to assume the function under test is side-effect free; if it is not, isolate it or reset relevant state between cases. After the run, a simple UART dump prints rows showing input, expected, actual, and pass/fail; you then know exactly which inputs produced unexpected results. Which case will you pick first to validate? Implementing a Test Table means a testcase struct plus a run loop provides repeatable, inspectable verification of function outputs on hardware.. In practical terms, a code-first walkthrough of the testcase structure and run loop.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: A TestCase struct plus a run loop provides repeatable, inspectable verification of function outputs on hardware.

content.html:
Process
Test table implementation
Key elements: struct, array, run loop, compare and mark pass flag.
typedef struct {
uint32_t input;
uint32_t expectedOutput;
uint32_t actualOutput;
uint8_t passed;
} TestCase;
TestCase tests[5] = { /* known inputs */ };
void runTests(void) { for each test call convert and set passed }
Checks and pitfalls
  • Reset shared state between cases if the function mutates global state.
  • Keep expected values authoritative and version-controlled.
  • Use clear UART formatting so rows are easy to parse by eye or script.
UART dump (simulated)
Input: 0 Expected:0 Actual:0 PASS Input:512 Expected:25 Actual:25 PASS Input:1023 Expected:50 Actual:49 FAIL Input:256 Expected:12 Actual:12 PASS Input:768 Expected:37 Actual:37 PASS
Example outcome
A single failing row points directly to the conversion logic. Use that input to step through the function in a debugger or add more focused tests around the failing branch.
Try this
Start with five cases covering low, mid, high, and two edge conditions. Run once, inspect the dump, then refine the cases where failures appear.

screens.title: SysTick Timer Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: The SysTick timer on Cortex-M processors is a simple 24-bit countdown counter designed for regular interrupts, but it is also very useful for timing short code segments. You initialize it by setting a reload value, clearing the current value, and enabling the timer with the core clock. To measure a code block, read the current value register before calling the function and then read it again after the function completes. Because the timer counts down, the elapsed cycles are computed by subtracting the second reading from the first. This method reports clock cycles, not wall-clock milliseconds, so you must convert cycles to time using your C P U clock rate when you want microseconds. A common trap is timer wraparound: if a long code path exceeds the timer range, the subtraction will be incorrect. For short measurements—small functions under test—wraparound is unlikely with the 24-bit range, but always be aware and add a guard for longer measurements. Using SysTick is far more accurate than measuring with software loops because it relies on a fixed hardware clock not subject to compiler optimization.

keyIdea.title: SysTick core idea
keyIdea.text: Sample the 24-bit countdown register before and after a call; compute elapsed cycles as start minus end and convert to time by dividing by clock frequency.

content.html:
Definition
SysTick timer
A 24-bit countdown timer that can be sampled to measure execution time in clock cycles.
  • Initialize: set reload, clear current, enable with core clock.
  • Measure: read current before and after, compute start minus end.
  • Convert: cycles divided by CPU frequency yield seconds.
Wraparound note
Because it counts down, if your measured section exceeds the timer range the result will be incorrect. For short functions the 24-bit range is usually sufficient, but you can guard for wrap by checking whether end is greater than start and adjusting accordingly.
Key Takeaway

SysTick provides reliable cycle counts for short measurements and is more accurate than timing via software loops.

Register pattern (visual)
NVIC_ST_CTRL_R = disable during setup; NVIC_ST_RELOAD_R = max reload; NVIC_ST_CURRENT_R = 0 to clear; NVIC_ST_CTRL_R = enable with core clock.
Sample usage
Call SysTick_Read() before and after the measured function and return start minus end to get elapsed cycles.
Practical example
Measure a small math routine or a recursive function for a few inputs to see how cycles change. This gives concrete data to prioritize optimizations.

screens.title: SysTick Initialization and Read Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the minimal steps required to use the SysTick timer for measurements. The pattern in the source sets the reload register to the maximum 24-bit value, clears the current value register, and then enables the timer with the core clock. A simple read routine returns the current value register. When timing, you sample before the function call to capture the starting count and sample again immediately after the call completes. Because SysTick counts down, subtract the ending reading from the starting reading to obtain elapsed cycles. The code pattern shown is intentionally minimal; you may add a guard for wraparound if you expect longer intervals. One subtle misconception is treating SysTick measurements as immune to interrupt effects: if interrupts occur during the measured region they will add cycles. For precise measurements isolate the measured code by disabling noncritical interrupts or account for interrupt cost in your analysis. After you get cycle counts, log them alongside input sizes to identify performance trends. keyIdea.title: Minimal pattern
keyIdea.text: Set reload, clear current, enable with clock, then read current value before and after the measured call and compute start minus end.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Init and read
NVIC_ST_CTRL_R = 0; NVIC_ST_RELOAD_R = 0x00FFFFFF; NVIC_ST_CURRENT_R = 0; NVIC_ST_CTRL_R = 0x05;
SysTick_Read simply returns the current value register. Use these two routines together to time calls.
Measurement caveat
Interrupts and context switches add cycles. For short deterministic measurements, run several iterations and take a median to reduce noise.
Visual timing flow
start = SysTick_Read(); call function; end = SysTick_Read(); elapsed = start - end;
Example use
Wrap the factorial or a sort routine and record cycle counts for increasing inputs to see scaling behavior.
Check your understanding
If a measured result is negative after subtraction, check for wrap or sampling order mistakes since SysTick counts down.

screens.title: Handling Timer Wraparound and Measurement Guards
screens.narratorSegment: While SysTick works well for short measurements, you must be mindful of wraparound and other pitfalls when measuring longer blocks. The timer is 24 bits and counts down, so measurements spanning a reload will appear incorrect if you simply subtract end from start without detecting wrap. A simple guard checks if the end sample is greater than the start sample; in that case add the reload value plus one to the computed difference to correct for the wrap. Another practical guard is to limit a single measured region to a range comfortably smaller than the reload to avoid wrap entirely. For noisy measurements, run multiple iterations and use a central tendency metric such as median rather than a single sample, because interrupts or cache effects can add spikes. A misconception is thinking timing always reveals algorithmic complexity directly; timing shows real cost on your platform including memory, branching, and interrupts, so interpret trends cautiously. Finally, log both cycles and the measured input so that performance plots correlate cost with input size and help you prioritize optimization choices. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Guard rules
keyIdea.text: Detect wraparound and use iteration-based sampling to reduce noise; correlate cycle counts with input sizes for useful analysis.

content.html:
Process Flow
Measurement guards
  1. 1. Choose a reload comfortably larger than expected measurement.
  2. 2. Sample start and end; if end > start, account for wrap by adding reload+1.
  3. 3. Repeat the measurement several times and take the median.
  4. 4. Correlate cycle counts with inputs to detect scaling patterns.
Example correction
If start is 1000 and end is 0x00FFFF00 (larger numerically), detect the wrap and compute elapsed as (start + (reload - end) + 1) or use a standard wrap formula.
Pro Tip

For short functions, pick a full reload and keep the measured window small; for longer tasks, measure in chunks and accumulate.

Noise reduction
Run 11 or more iterations and choose the median; remove outliers caused by interrupts or cache misses to see consistent cost.
Plot cycles for inputs 1,5,10,15 to identify whether cost grows linearly, quadratically, or shows plateaus due to cache or peripheral waits.
Check your understanding
If your measured cycles increase irregularly, consider whether interrupts or hardware involvement, not just algorithmic complexity, are causing variation.

screens.title: Assertions and Sanity Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Assertions are a defensive programming technique that verify assumptions at runtime and report failures during development. In embedded projects a minimal assertion macro can send an error message and halt the system, making it clear where the program's invariants failed. The example macro sends a serial text message containing the literal 'ASSERTION FAILED at line' followed by the failing source line number and then enters a tight loop to stop further execution. This immediate fail-fast behavior prevents subtle corruption from propagating and makes root-cause diagnosis much easier. During production builds you typically disable assertions so they compile to nothing for performance and code size considerations. A misconception is that assertions are a substitute for error handling; they are not. Assertions check programmer assumptions and invariants, while normal error handling deals with expected runtime conditions such as peripheral timeouts. Use assertions liberally in development, but design your runtime error handling separately for production reliability. keyIdea.title: Assertion role
keyIdea.text: Assertions validate programmer assumptions during development, reporting location and halting to make debugging straightforward.

content.html:
Definition
Assertion macro
A development-time check that reports a failing condition and halts execution to aid debugging.
Behavior: if condition is false, send a clear message over UART with line number and stop in an infinite loop so developers can inspect state.
Development vs Production
Enable assertions during development builds. In production define the macro to nothing to avoid halting behavior and minimize code size.
Example run
ASSERT(false) → UART: ASSERTION FAILED at line 123 → system halts. Use the line number to locate the faulty assumption.
Common pitfalls
  • Don't rely on assertions for expected user input errors; handle those with normal error handling.
  • Be careful halting in safety-critical systems; use a development-only channel or fallback when needed.
Key Takeaway

Assertions give immediate, precise failure signals during development so you can fix incorrect assumptions quickly.

screens.title: Lab: Factorial Tests and Timing
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on practice ties the chapter together. Implement a factorial function and create a test table with inputs and expected outputs for values such as 1, 5, 10, and 15. Run the test harness to populate actual outputs and send the table over UART so you can confirm correctness for each case. screens.title: SysTick vs Software Delay Loops
screens.narratorSegment: You will often be asked whether a software delay loop is sufficient for measuring execution time. A software delay loop counts instructions or iterations in software, and its timing depends heavily on compiler optimizations, instruction scheduling, and even code placement. In contrast, the SysTick hardware timer runs at the core clock and provides a fixed reference independent of compiler behavior. This makes SysTick measurements repeatable and trustworthy. For example, if a loop compiles to a different instruction sequence on a new toolchain, measured durations from software loops may change even though the algorithm is identical. A common misunderstanding is assuming software timing is stable across builds; it's not. Hardware timers like SysTick remain consistent, and they report cycles that you can convert to time precisely given the C P U frequency. Use software loops only for crude delays or when no timer is available. fullNarratorScript:
In embedded systems we often cannot look inside the running program the way we do on a desktop. This chapter equips you with practical techniques to observe what your code actually does, measure how long functions take, and stop errors before they cascade. You will learn functional debugging: building small test tables, running them on the hardware, and dumping results to the serial port or debugger to verify correctness. You will also learn how to use the processor SysTick timer to measure execution time in clock cycles, how to interpret those counts, and when wraparound matters. Finally, you will add simple assertion checks that report failures immediately during development. These techniques are complementary: test tables give you functional confidence, SysTick gives you quantitative performance data, and assertions let you catch invalid states early. Together they make embedded debugging systematic instead of accidental. As you proceed, keep a small test harness and a short timing routine handy. That combination will save hours verifying behavior on hardware. Consider which of these you will try first on your next lab board.

Over the next screens you'll learn four practical skills that make embedded debugging reliable. First, functional debugging: you'll build small test tables that capture inputs, expected outputs, and actual outputs, then run them on hardware and dump the results to the serial port. This gives repeatable evidence that a function behaves correctly for representative inputs. Second, you will measure execution time using the SysTick hardware timer. You will initialize the timer, sample its current value before and after a call, and compute the difference in clock cycles. Third, you'll analyze function performance by counting clock cycles across inputs to see how cost scales. This is how you move from guesswork to data-driven optimization. Fourth, you'll implement assertion macros that report the failing line and halt execution during development so errors are detected immediately. Each objective ties to hands-on checks: a test harness, a short timing routine, cycle-count comparisons, and an assertion-enabled build. These are concrete practices you can add to everyday embedded workflows to save debugging time and avoid subtle runtime errors.

Now let's translate those objectives into demonstrable practice. For functional debugging, prepare a small array of test cases that include input, expected output, actual output, and a pass flag. Run the tests on your board and dump the array to UART to inspect results. For SysTick measurement, write a tiny measurement wrapper that reads the timer before and after the function and returns the difference in cycles. Use that wrapper to time functions with representative inputs and record the counts. For cycle counting, gather results into a small table and plot or list them so you can compare trends. For assertions, implement a macro that emits an error message and halts when a condition is false during development; make it compile to nothing in production builds. These are the testable behaviors you will show in labs. Each step is short, repeatable, and lends itself to automation so you can re-run tests after changes and trust the results.

Functional debugging is a pragmatic strategy to make program behavior visible on devices without rich UI or file systems. At its core you construct a small table of test cases: each entry records the input, the expected output, a slot for actual output, and a pass flag. You run the tests on the target hardware, populate actual outputs, and then transmit the table over the serial port or inspect it in the debugger. This approach turns an invisible internal computation into concrete, repeatable evidence. For example, a temperature conversion function can be validated by providing five known analog readings and their correct temperatures; after running the harness you will immediately see which entries match and which do not. A common misconception is that functional debugging replaces unit testing frameworks; instead it is a form of unit testing adapted for hardware constraints. The value is that you can reproduce edge cases on the real device and see real outputs rather than simulated results. Key practice: keep test cases small, deterministic, and representative so failures point directly to the function under test. How will you structure your first test table?

Let's review a compact implementation pattern for a test table and the run loop that populates actual outputs. The pattern uses a small struct with four fields: input, expected output, actual output, and a pass flag. You initialize an array of these structs with known inputs and expected results, leaving actual output and the pass flag unset. The run loop calls the function under test for each input, stores the returned value in actual output, then compares it to expected to set the pass flag. This approach is explicit and easy to inspect on hardware. One practical tip is to keep the table small—five to ten representative cases—so the UART dump remains readable. A common error is to assume the function under test is side-effect free; if it is not, isolate it or reset relevant state between cases. After the run, a simple UART dump prints rows showing input, expected, actual, and pass/fail; you then know exactly which inputs produced unexpected results. The SysTick timer on Cortex-M processors is a simple 24-bit countdown counter designed for regular interrupts, but it is also very useful for timing short code segments. You initialize it by setting a reload value, clearing the current value, and enabling the timer with the core clock. To measure a code block, read the current value register before calling the function and then read it again after the function completes. Because the timer counts down, the elapsed cycles are computed by subtracting the second reading from the first. This method reports clock cycles, not wall-clock milliseconds, so you must convert cycles to time using your C P U clock rate when you want microseconds. A common trap is timer wraparound: if a long code path exceeds the timer range, the subtraction will be incorrect. For short measurements—small functions under test—wraparound is unlikely with the 24-bit range, but always be aware and add a guard for longer measurements. Using SysTick is far more accurate than measuring with software loops because it relies on a fixed hardware clock not subject to compiler optimization.

The pattern in the source sets the reload register to the maximum 24-bit value, clears the current value register, and then enables the timer with the core clock. A simple read routine returns the current value register. When timing, you sample before the function call to capture the starting count and sample again immediately after the call completes. Because SysTick counts down, subtract the ending reading from the starting reading to obtain elapsed cycles. The timer is 24 bits and counts down, so measurements spanning a reload will appear incorrect if you simply subtract end from start without detecting wrap. A simple guard checks if the end sample is greater than the start sample; in that case add the reload value plus one to the computed difference to correct for the wrap. Before you finish a debugging or profiling session, run this concise checklist to ensure both correctness and meaningful performance data. First, build a small test table with representative inputs and expected outputs. Run the tests and dump results to UART to confirm correctness. Second, instrument the function with a SysTick measurement wrapper and run multiple iterations per input, collecting medians to reduce noise. Third, check for wraparound and correct any measurements that cross the SysTick boundary. Fourth, add assertions for key invariants to catch unexpected states in future runs. Fifth, compile the cycle data into a short table or plot and ask whether the function meets timing requirements or needs optimization. Finally, document the environment: C P U frequency, interrupt status, and whether tests were run with caching or peripherals active. Keep four core ideas in mind. First, functional debugging turns hidden program state into a small, inspectable dataset by using test tables and UART dumps. Second, the SysTick timer is a hardware countdown counter you can sample before and after a function to obtain cycle counts that convert to time with the C P U frequency. Third, assertions help you detect broken assumptions quickly during development by reporting a line number and halting execution. Fourth, use data-driven performance analysis: measure cycles across representative inputs, use medians to reduce noise, and prioritize optimizations where cycle counts show the largest payoff. These tools form a practical workflow: verify correctness with tests, measure cost with hardware timers, and guard assumptions with assertions. Third, add assertions to catch incorrect assumptions early in development; they should halt and report the failing location so you can inspect state immediately.
